examples.title: Selecting Columns
examples.description: Choose specific columns from a table
examples.markdown:
## Selecting columns

`select` builds a new table containing only the columns you name, in the order you name them. The original table is left untouched. That is true of every `Table` method.

Step through the visualization and notice that the number of rows never changes; only the columns do.
cells: from datascience import *

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = Table().with_columns(
    'Flavor', make_array('strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'),
    'Color', make_array('pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'),
    'Price', make_array(3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50)
)
cones

# Just the flavor and the price
cones.select('Flavor', 'Price')

examples.title: Filtering Rows
examples.description: Keep only rows that match a condition
examples.markdown:
## Filtering rows with `where`

`where(column, value)` keeps only the rows whose value in that column matches. Here we keep the chocolate cones.

As you step through, watch each row get checked against the condition: kept rows are highlighted, and the ones that don't match are struck through before they disappear from the result.
cells: from datascience import *

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = Table().with_columns(
    'Flavor', make_array('strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'),
    'Color', make_array('pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'),
    'Price', make_array(3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50)
)
cones

# Only the chocolate cones
chocolate = cones.where('Flavor', 'chocolate')
chocolate

examples.title: Sorting by Values
examples.description: Order rows by a column
examples.markdown:
## Sorting rows

`sort(column)` orders the rows by a column, smallest first. Passing `descending=True` flips that, so the highest salary comes out on top.

Every row survives a sort. Only their order changes. Watch the rows move in the step-through.
cells: from datascience import *

# Salaries in millions of dollars for a few players
nba = Table().with_columns(
    'PLAYER', make_array('Stephen Curry', 'Klay Thompson', 'Draymond Green', 'LeBron James', 'Anthony Davis', 'Kawhi Leonard', 'Damian Lillard'),
    'POSITION', make_array('PG', 'SG', 'PF', 'SF', 'PF', 'SF', 'PG'),
    'TEAM', make_array('Golden State Warriors', 'Golden State Warriors', 'Golden State Warriors', 'Los Angeles Lakers', 'Los Angeles Lakers', 'Los Angeles Clippers', 'Portland Trail Blazers'),
    'SALARY', make_array(40.2, 32.7, 18.5, 37.4, 27.1, 32.7, 29.8)
)
nba

# Highest paid first
nba.sort('SALARY', descending=True)

examples.title: Adding a Column
examples.description: Add a new column to the table
examples.markdown:
## Adding a column

`with_column(label, values)` returns a copy of the table with one more column. The array of values must have exactly one entry per row, in row order.

Here the new column is built from an existing one: the price with sales tax. Watch it appear on the right of the result.
cells: from datascience import *

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = Table().with_columns(
    'Flavor', make_array('strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'),
    'Color', make_array('pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'),
    'Price', make_array(3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50)
)
cones

# Price including 9% sales tax, one value per row
with_tax = cones.column('Price') * 1.09
cones.with_column('Price with Tax', with_tax)

examples.title: Dropping Columns
examples.description: Remove columns from a table
examples.markdown:
## Dropping columns

`drop` is the mirror image of `select`: you name the columns you want to get rid of, and everything else stays.

Use it when a table has many columns and it is easier to say what you don't need.
cells: from datascience import *

# Tall buildings: height in meters and the year they were completed
skyscrapers = Table().with_columns(
    'name', make_array('One World Trade Center', 'Willis Tower', 'Empire State Building', 'Salesforce Tower', 'Aon Center', 'Transamerica Pyramid', '30 Hudson Yards'),
    'material', make_array('composite', 'steel', 'steel', 'composite', 'steel', 'concrete', 'composite'),
    'city', make_array('New York City', 'Chicago', 'New York City', 'San Francisco', 'Chicago', 'San Francisco', 'New York City'),
    'height', make_array(541, 442, 381, 326, 346, 260, 387),
    'completed', make_array(2014, 1974, 1931, 2018, 1973, 1972, 2019)
)
skyscrapers

# Keep everything except the material and the year
skyscrapers.drop('material', 'completed')

examples.title: Grouping and Counting
examples.description: Count how many rows share each value
examples.markdown:
## Grouping and counting

`group(column)` collects the rows that share a value in the column and counts them. Every distinct flavor becomes one row of the result, with a `count` column.

Step through it: first the rows are gathered by flavor, then each group collapses into one row.
cells: from datascience import *

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = Table().with_columns(
    'Flavor', make_array('strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'),
    'Color', make_array('pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'),
    'Price', make_array(3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50)
)
cones

# How many cones of each flavor
cones.group('Flavor')

examples.title: Joining Tables
examples.description: Combine two tables on a common column
examples.markdown:
## Joining two tables

`join(column, other_table)` matches rows from two tables that share a value in the named column and lines them up side by side.

Both tables have a cafe name. Watch the second table appear under the first, with matching cafes highlighted as each row is paired up. A cafe that appears in only one table is dropped.
cells: from datascience import *

# Drinks sold at cafes near campus
drinks = Table().with_columns(
    'Drink', make_array('Milk Tea', 'Espresso', 'Latte', 'Espresso'),
    'Cafe', make_array('Asha', 'Strada', 'Strada', 'FSM'),
    'Price', make_array(4.00, 2.00, 3.00, 2.00)
)
drinks

# Coupons that some cafes accept
discounts = Table().with_columns(
    'Coupon % off', make_array(10, 25, 5),
    'Location', make_array('Asha', 'Strada', 'Asha')
)
discounts

# Pair each drink with every coupon its cafe accepts
drinks.join('Cafe', discounts, 'Location')

examples.title: Chaining Operations
examples.description: Combine multiple operations in sequence
examples.markdown:
## Chaining operations

Because every `Table` method returns a new table, you can call another method on the result right away. Wrapping the expression in parentheses lets you put each step on its own line.

Read it top to bottom: keep the Warriors, keep only player and salary, then sort. The visualization shows one step per method call.
cells: from datascience import *

# Salaries in millions of dollars for a few players
nba = Table().with_columns(
    'PLAYER', make_array('Stephen Curry', 'Klay Thompson', 'Draymond Green', 'LeBron James', 'Anthony Davis', 'Kawhi Leonard', 'Damian Lillard'),
    'POSITION', make_array('PG', 'SG', 'PF', 'SF', 'PF', 'SF', 'PG'),
    'TEAM', make_array('Golden State Warriors', 'Golden State Warriors', 'Golden State Warriors', 'Los Angeles Lakers', 'Los Angeles Lakers', 'Los Angeles Clippers', 'Portland Trail Blazers'),
    'SALARY', make_array(40.2, 32.7, 18.5, 37.4, 27.1, 32.7, 29.8)
)
nba

# Warriors, highest paid first
warriors = (nba
    .where('TEAM', 'Golden State Warriors')
    .select('PLAYER', 'SALARY')
    .sort('SALARY', descending=True))
warriors

examples.title: Multiple Filters
examples.description: Apply multiple where conditions
examples.markdown:
## Filtering twice

A second `where` on the result of the first narrows things down further. `are.above(30)` is a *predicate*, a reusable condition, from the `are` collection.

Compare the two filter steps: the first checks the Destination column, the second checks the delay against a threshold.
cells: from datascience import *

# United flights out of SFO: delay in minutes (negative means early)
united = Table().with_columns(
    'Date', make_array('6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/2/15', '6/2/15', '6/2/15', '6/3/15'),
    'Flight Number', make_array(73, 217, 237, 250, 267, 273, 290, 73),
    'Destination', make_array('HNL', 'EWR', 'STL', 'SAN', 'PHL', 'SEA', 'JFK', 'HNL'),
    'Delay', make_array(257, 28, -3, 0, 64, -6, 12, 5)
)
united

# Flights to Hawaii
to_hnl = united.where('Destination', 'HNL')
to_hnl

# Of those, the ones more than half an hour late
late = to_hnl.where('Delay', are.above(30))
late

examples.title: Pivot Tables
examples.description: Reshape data with pivot operations
examples.markdown:
## Pivoting

`pivot(columns, rows, values, function)` turns one column's values into column headers and another's into row labels, then fills each cell by aggregating the `values` column.

Here every material becomes a column and every city a row, and each cell is the tallest building of that kind in that city. Step through to see the source rows feed each cell.
cells: from datascience import *

# Tall buildings: height in meters and the year they were completed
skyscrapers = Table().with_columns(
    'name', make_array('One World Trade Center', 'Willis Tower', 'Empire State Building', 'Salesforce Tower', 'Aon Center', 'Transamerica Pyramid', '30 Hudson Yards'),
    'material', make_array('composite', 'steel', 'steel', 'composite', 'steel', 'concrete', 'composite'),
    'city', make_array('New York City', 'Chicago', 'New York City', 'San Francisco', 'Chicago', 'San Francisco', 'New York City'),
    'height', make_array(541, 442, 381, 326, 346, 260, 387),
    'completed', make_array(2014, 1974, 1931, 2018, 1973, 1972, 2019)
)
skyscrapers

# Tallest building by city and material
skyscrapers.pivot('material', 'city', 'height', max)

examples.title: Group with a Function
examples.description: Group by column and summarize the others
examples.markdown:
## Different aggregates on the same groups

The function you pass to `group` decides what each group collapses to. `np.average` gives the average salary per team; `max` gives the highest.

The groups are identical in both calls. Only the number in the salary column changes, and so does its name: `SALARY average` versus `SALARY max`.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np

# Salaries in millions of dollars for a few players
nba = Table().with_columns(
    'PLAYER', make_array('Stephen Curry', 'Klay Thompson', 'Draymond Green', 'LeBron James', 'Anthony Davis', 'Kawhi Leonard', 'Damian Lillard'),
    'POSITION', make_array('PG', 'SG', 'PF', 'SF', 'PF', 'SF', 'PG'),
    'TEAM', make_array('Golden State Warriors', 'Golden State Warriors', 'Golden State Warriors', 'Los Angeles Lakers', 'Los Angeles Lakers', 'Los Angeles Clippers', 'Portland Trail Blazers'),
    'SALARY', make_array(40.2, 32.7, 18.5, 37.4, 27.1, 32.7, 29.8)
)
nba

# Average salary on each team
nba.select('TEAM', 'SALARY').group('TEAM', np.average)

# Highest salary on each team
nba.select('TEAM', 'SALARY').group('TEAM', max)

examples.title: Joining Films with Studios
examples.description: Add information about each film from a second table
examples.markdown:
## Joining on a studio name

`Studio` is the key that links a film to the company that made it. `join` pairs each film with the row in `studios` that has the same name.

Watch the keys get matched one at a time, and notice the joined table keeps the columns from both.
cells: from datascience import *

# Highest-grossing films, gross in millions of dollars
top = Table().with_columns(
    'Title', make_array('Star Wars', 'E.T.', 'Titanic', 'Jurassic Park', 'The Lion King', 'Avatar', 'Jaws'),
    'Studio', make_array('Fox', 'Universal', 'Paramount', 'Universal', 'Buena Vista', 'Fox', 'Universal'),
    'Gross', make_array(461, 435, 659, 402, 423, 761, 260),
    'Year', make_array(1977, 1982, 1997, 1993, 1994, 2009, 1975)
)
top

# Where each studio is based
studios = Table().with_columns(
    'Studio', make_array('Fox', 'Universal', 'Paramount', 'Buena Vista'),
    'Founded', make_array(1935, 1912, 1912, 1953)
)
studios

# Each film with its studio's founding year
top.join('Studio', studios)

examples.title: A Full Pipeline
examples.description: Filter, select, group and sort in one expression
examples.markdown:
## A full pipeline

This is the shape of most real analyses: filter down to the rows you care about, select the useful columns, group to summarise, and sort to rank.

Watch how the table changes character at each step, from individual buildings to one row per city. The sort uses `height max`, the column that `group` created.
cells: from datascience import *

# Tall buildings: height in meters and the year they were completed
skyscrapers = Table().with_columns(
    'name', make_array('One World Trade Center', 'Willis Tower', 'Empire State Building', 'Salesforce Tower', 'Aon Center', 'Transamerica Pyramid', '30 Hudson Yards'),
    'material', make_array('composite', 'steel', 'steel', 'composite', 'steel', 'concrete', 'composite'),
    'city', make_array('New York City', 'Chicago', 'New York City', 'San Francisco', 'Chicago', 'San Francisco', 'New York City'),
    'height', make_array(541, 442, 381, 326, 346, 260, 387),
    'completed', make_array(2014, 1974, 1931, 2018, 1973, 1972, 2019)
)
skyscrapers

# Tallest modern building in each city, tallest city first
result = (skyscrapers
    .where('completed', are.above(1970))
    .select('city', 'height')
    .group('city', max)
    .sort('height max', descending=True))
result

examples.title: Taking Rows by Position
examples.description: Pick rows by their position
examples.markdown:
## Taking rows by position

`take(n)` returns the row at position `n`, and `take(np.arange(3))` returns positions 0, 1 and 2. Row positions start at 0.

Sorting first makes `take` useful: the top three grossing films are the first three rows of the sorted table.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np

# Highest-grossing films, gross in millions of dollars
top = Table().with_columns(
    'Title', make_array('Star Wars', 'E.T.', 'Titanic', 'Jurassic Park', 'The Lion King', 'Avatar', 'Jaws'),
    'Studio', make_array('Fox', 'Universal', 'Paramount', 'Universal', 'Buena Vista', 'Fox', 'Universal'),
    'Gross', make_array(461, 435, 659, 402, 423, 761, 260),
    'Year', make_array(1977, 1982, 1997, 1993, 1994, 2009, 1975)
)
top

# Top three by gross
top.sort('Gross', descending=True).take(np.arange(3))

examples.title: Pivot with Sums
examples.description: Totals for every pair of categories
examples.markdown:
## Pivoting to totals

Each cell of the pivot is the sum of population over the rows that share that country and year. Because every country appears once per year here, each cell holds exactly one value.

Step through and check that every (country, year) pair from the original table lands in exactly one cell.
cells: from datascience import *

# Population in millions
population = Table().with_columns(
    'Country', make_array('Brazil', 'Brazil', 'Kenya', 'Kenya', 'Japan', 'Japan'),
    'Year', make_array(2000, 2010, 2000, 2010, 2000, 2010),
    'Population', make_array(175, 196, 31, 42, 127, 128)
)
population

# One column per year, one row per country
population.pivot('Year', 'Country', 'Population', sum)

examples.title: Average versus Maximum
examples.description: Summarize groups two different ways
examples.markdown:
## Average versus maximum delay

Grouping by destination with `np.average` gives the typical delay; grouping with `max` gives the worst one. The groups are the same, the summary differs.

Notice the group step happens first in both calls, and the aggregation happens after.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np

# United flights out of SFO: delay in minutes (negative means early)
united = Table().with_columns(
    'Date', make_array('6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/2/15', '6/2/15', '6/2/15', '6/3/15'),
    'Flight Number', make_array(73, 217, 237, 250, 267, 273, 290, 73),
    'Destination', make_array('HNL', 'EWR', 'STL', 'SAN', 'PHL', 'SEA', 'JFK', 'HNL'),
    'Delay', make_array(257, 28, -3, 0, 64, -6, 12, 5)
)
united

# Typical delay per destination
united.select('Destination', 'Delay').group('Destination', np.average)

# Worst delay per destination
united.select('Destination', 'Delay').group('Destination', max)

examples.title: Multi-Step Data Analysis
examples.description: Complete workflow: filter, group, sort, and select
examples.markdown:
## Filter, group, sort, select

A four-step analysis, one method at a time. Keep the babies born to non-smokers, average each column, and read off the typical birth weight.

Watch the `Maternal Smoker` column disappear after the group step: once rows are collapsed into groups, only the grouped column and the summaries remain.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np

# Newborns: birth weight in ounces, pregnancy length in days, whether the mother smoked
baby = Table().with_columns(
    'Birth Weight', make_array(120, 113, 128, 108, 136, 138, 132, 120, 143, 140, 144, 141),
    'Gestational Days', make_array(284, 282, 279, 282, 286, 244, 245, 289, 299, 351, 282, 279),
    'Maternal Smoker', make_array(False, False, True, True, False, False, False, False, False, True, False, False)
)
baby

# Babies whose mothers did not smoke
non_smokers = baby.where('Maternal Smoker', False)
non_smokers

# Average of every column, for smokers and non-smokers
averages = baby.group('Maternal Smoker', np.average)
averages

# Heaviest group first
by_weight = averages.sort('Birth Weight average', descending=True)
by_weight

# Just the columns worth reporting
by_weight.select('Maternal Smoker', 'Birth Weight average')

examples.title: Scatter Plot
examples.description: Plot two numerical columns against each other
examples.markdown:
## Scatter plot

`scatter(x_column, y_column)` draws one point per row. It is the first thing to try when you want to know whether two numerical variables are related.

`fit_line=True` adds the least-squares regression line. Galton's question: do taller parents have taller children? Look at how closely the points follow the line.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plots
plots.style.use('fivethirtyeight')

# Galton's families: heights in inches of a parent and their adult child
heights = Table().with_columns(
    'Parent Average', make_array(72.7, 70.5, 69.0, 66.5, 65.5, 64.0, 68.0, 71.0),
    'Child', make_array(73.2, 69.2, 69.0, 66.5, 64.0, 63.5, 68.5, 70.0)
)
heights

# One point per family, plus the line of best fit
heights.scatter('Parent Average', 'Child', fit_line=True)

examples.title: Histogram
examples.description: See the distribution of one numerical column
examples.markdown:
## Histogram

`hist(column, bins=...)` shows how the values of one column are distributed. Each bar covers a bin, and the bins are half-open: the bin `[120, 130)` contains 120 up to but not including 130.

The vertical axis is percent per unit, so the *area* of a bar is the percent of rows in that bin. That is why the bars stay comparable even when bins have different widths.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plots
plots.style.use('fivethirtyeight')

# Newborns: birth weight in ounces, pregnancy length in days, whether the mother smoked
baby = Table().with_columns(
    'Birth Weight', make_array(120, 113, 128, 108, 136, 138, 132, 120, 143, 140, 144, 141),
    'Gestational Days', make_array(284, 282, 279, 282, 286, 244, 245, 289, 299, 351, 282, 279),
    'Maternal Smoker', make_array(False, False, True, True, False, False, False, False, False, True, False, False)
)
baby

# Birth weights in bins of 10 ounces
baby.hist('Birth Weight', bins=np.arange(100, 151, 10))

examples.title: Bar Chart
examples.description: Compare counts across categories
examples.markdown:
## Bar chart

Categorical data is summarised with `group`, which produces one row per category and a `count` column. `barh(category_column)` then draws one horizontal bar per row, using the category column for the labels and the remaining numerical columns for the bar lengths.

Sorting the grouped table first makes the chart easier to read. Step through the visualization to watch the rows collapse into groups before the chart is drawn.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plots
plots.style.use('fivethirtyeight')

# Highest-grossing films, gross in millions of dollars
top = Table().with_columns(
    'Title', make_array('Star Wars', 'E.T.', 'Titanic', 'Jurassic Park', 'The Lion King', 'Avatar', 'Jaws'),
    'Studio', make_array('Fox', 'Universal', 'Paramount', 'Universal', 'Buena Vista', 'Fox', 'Universal'),
    'Gross', make_array(461, 435, 659, 402, 423, 761, 260),
    'Year', make_array(1977, 1982, 1997, 1993, 1994, 2009, 1975)
)
top

# How many of the top films each studio made
by_studio = top.group('Studio')
by_studio

# Largest first, then one bar per row
by_studio.sort('count', descending=True).barh('Studio')

examples.title: Applying a Function
examples.description: Call a function on every row: one column, two columns, or the whole row
examples.markdown:
## Applying a function to every row

`apply(function, column)` calls the function once per row, passing in that row's value from the column, and collects the results in an array. The array is not a table: it has no column label of its own, and it lives outside the table until you put it back in with `with_column`.

Three ways to call it, each shown below:

- **one column**: `apply(to_feet, 'height')` passes one value per row;
- **two columns**: `apply(describe, 'name', 'city')` passes two values per row, in the order the labels are given, so the function needs two parameters;
- **the whole row**: `apply(is_recent)` with no column passes the entire row, and the function reads what it needs with `row.item('completed')`.

Step through the visualization and watch the function run on one row at a time.
cells: from datascience import *

# Tall buildings: height in meters and the year they were completed
skyscrapers = Table().with_columns(
    'name', make_array('One World Trade Center', 'Willis Tower', 'Empire State Building', 'Salesforce Tower', 'Aon Center', 'Transamerica Pyramid', '30 Hudson Yards'),
    'material', make_array('composite', 'steel', 'steel', 'composite', 'steel', 'concrete', 'composite'),
    'city', make_array('New York City', 'Chicago', 'New York City', 'San Francisco', 'Chicago', 'San Francisco', 'New York City'),
    'height', make_array(541, 442, 381, 326, 346, 260, 387),
    'completed', make_array(2014, 1974, 1931, 2018, 1973, 1972, 2019)
)
skyscrapers

# Put the array back into the table as a new column
skyscrapers.with_column('height (ft)', feet)

# Two columns: the function gets two values per row, in the order the labels are listed
def describe(name, city):
    return name + ' in ' + city

skyscrapers.apply(describe, 'name', 'city')

# No column named: the whole row is passed in
def is_recent(row):
    return row.item('completed') >= 2010

skyscrapers.apply(is_recent)

examples.title: Random Sample
examples.description: Draw rows at random, with or without replacement
examples.markdown:
## Sampling rows

`sample(k)` draws `k` rows at random. By default it draws **with replacement**: after each draw the row goes back in, so the same flight can show up more than once. `sample(k, with_replacement=False)` draws each row at most once. `shuffle()` is a sample of every row without replacement, which just puts the table in a random order.

The seed makes the random draws repeatable, so the visualization matches what you see when you run it. Step through to watch each draw pick a row and copy it into the result.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(8)

# United flights out of SFO: delay in minutes (negative means early)
united = Table().with_columns(
    'Date', make_array('6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/1/15', '6/2/15', '6/2/15', '6/2/15', '6/3/15'),
    'Flight Number', make_array(73, 217, 237, 250, 267, 273, 290, 73),
    'Destination', make_array('HNL', 'EWR', 'STL', 'SAN', 'PHL', 'SEA', 'JFK', 'HNL'),
    'Delay', make_array(257, 28, -3, 0, 64, -6, 12, 5)
)
united

# Five draws with replacement: expect some repeats
united.sample(5)

# Three draws without replacement: no repeats possible
united.sample(3, with_replacement=False)

# Every row once, in random order
united.shuffle()

examples.title: Splitting a Table
examples.description: Randomly divide rows into two tables
examples.markdown:
## Splitting into two tables

`split(k)` shuffles the rows and then divides them: the first `k` go into one table and the rest into another. Every row lands in exactly one of the two, so the row counts add up to the original.

This is how a dataset gets divided into a training set and a test set. `split` returns two tables, so the cell unpacks them into two names.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(2)

# Galton's families: heights in inches of a parent and their adult child
heights = Table().with_columns(
    'Parent Average', make_array(72.7, 70.5, 69.0, 66.5, 65.5, 64.0, 68.0, 71.0),
    'Child', make_array(73.2, 69.2, 69.0, 66.5, 64.0, 63.5, 68.5, 70.0)
)
heights

# Five families to fit a line on, the other three to test it
train, test = heights.split(5)
train
test

examples.title: Column vs Select
examples.description: A table with one column is not the same as an array of values
examples.markdown:
## `select` gives a table, `column` gives an array

Two calls that look alike do very different things. `select('Price')` returns a **table** that happens to have one column: it still has a label, rows, and all the table methods. `column('Price')` returns an **array**: just the values, in order, with no label.

Arrays are what arithmetic and numpy functions work on. `np.average(prices)` works; `np.average(price_table)` does not. Step through to see the difference in shape on the right.
cells:
from datascience import *
import numpy as np

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = Table().with_columns(
    'Flavor', make_array('strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'),
    'Color', make_array('pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'),
    'Price', make_array(3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50)
)
cones

# A table with one column
price_table = cones.select('Price')
price_table

# An array of values
prices = cones.column('Price')
prices

# Arrays are what arithmetic and numpy work on
np.average(prices)
